newsitem.title: UK: Britain to ban most handguns after Dunblane.
newsitem.headline: Britain to ban most handguns after Dunblane.

text.p: The British government was expected on Wednesday to propose an almost complete ban on handguns following the Dunblane massacre in March when crazed loner Thomas Hamilton shot dead 16 children and their teacher.

According to media reports, the only handguns Britons would be allowed to hold under the government's proposals would be single-shot .22 inch calibre weapons, widely used in shooting competitions. These would have to be kept at gun clubs.
A spokesman at Prime Minister John Major's office said he could not confirm the plan ahead of government statements to parliament at 1430 gmt.
"The government will set out its views to the House (of Commons) this afternoon. We cannot pre-empt that," he said.
Major on Tuesday called a meeting of senior ministers to discuss the government's response to a report on Dunblane drawn up by senior Scottish judge Lord Douglas Cullen.

Cullen is widely believed to have recommended that handguns -- four of which Hamilton used in his attack on a primary school in the Scottish town of Dunblane -- should be restricted to those kept at registered gun clubs.

But according to the reports, Major, pressed by Scottish secretary Michael Forsyth, whose own parliamentary constituency includes Dunblane, decided to go much further and institute an almost total ban.

The issue of gun control is an emotive subject in Britain following the slaughter of the innocents at Dunblane by a man known as a loner with a worrying fondness for young boys and who believed he was being persecuted.
Campaigners for a complete ban on handguns have collected 750,000 signatures on a petition putting their case, and have won the backing of the opposition Labour Party.
Although gun ownership is relatively rare in Britain, opinion polls show around 70 percent of the population want a total handgun ban.
Gun lobbyists say the vast majority of the 57,000 holders of handgun licences practise target shooting and other legitimate activities, and should not suffer for Hamilton's actions.

Rosemary Hunter, one of the organisers of the anti-gun petition, told BBC radio on Wednesday that if .22 weapons, which currently account for 10 percent of British handguns, remain legal, another Dunblane could not be ruled out.
"Someone with Hamilton's mentality can simply book the weapon out (for a competition at another gun club) and then...commit such an atrocity as we saw on March 13," she said.

The National Union of Teachers agreed. "It has to be right that handguns are banned. It is a pity the Government is not going the whole way and banning them completely," said general secretary Doug McAvoy.
And Conservative member of parliament David Mellor, a former interior minister, said the government should have acted months ago to curb handgun ownership.
"If we adopt the American way of life, we have to come to terms with the American way of death," he said.

But Michael Yardley, a columnist for the Shooting Times magazine, described the government's expected decision as "intellectual nonsense", saying the real need was to reduce the thousands of weapons illegally held by criminals.
If the government pushes through restrictions on handguns, it will be the second time within months that a developed country has cracked down on firearms following a mass slaughter.

In July, Australian Prime Minister John Howard won national agreement to laws banning self-loading guns and tightening firearm ownership rules after 35 people were shot dead at the Port Arthur tourist site on the island of Tasmania on April 28.
